Installation and setup

Source: vignettes/example5.Rmd
example5.Rmd

bayesnec fits its models with brms (Bürkner 2017; Bürkner 2018), which passes them to Stan (https://mc-stan.org/). Stan does not interpret a model. Each model is translated into C++, compiled into a program, and that program is run. A C++ toolchain is therefore required to fit anything at all, and this is also why the first fit of a session takes longer than the ones after it.

brms samples through either of two back ends. rstan (Stan Development Team 2020) is installed as a dependency of brms whether or not it is used as the sampler, so it is present on any machine that can load brms. cmdstanr is on neither CRAN nor the dependency list of bayesnec, and is what this package’s own vignettes are built with; options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr") is the line that selects it. The instructions below install cmdstanr. The rstan route is documented by the Stan project at https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started.

Software requirements

Software Purpose
R the language the package runs in
A C++ toolchain compiles each model before it is fitted
CmdStan the sampler that runs the compiled model

The toolchain is the part that differs by operating system, and the part that fails most often. On Windows it is Rtools, on macOS the Xcode Command Line Tools, and on Linux the standard build tools.

Route by operating system

Windows needs the most care, and has its own section below. The difficulties Stan had on Windows historically came from rstan, which requires matched versions of several compiled packages. cmdstanr avoids most of that, and what remains is the toolchain and the installation path.

Linux needs the least. A current distribution’s build tools are already what Stan requires, and the default installation path raises none of the problems the Windows section deals with.

macOS has not been verified for these instructions, so its section points at the instructions the projects themselves maintain.

What determines whether an installation works is the check in the Verification section, not which of these routes was followed to reach it.

Windows

R and Rtools

Install R first, from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/, and then the Rtools that matches it, from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/. Accept the default installation location.

Rtools is versioned against the minor version of R, and CRAN’s Rtools page states which Rtools goes with which R. A mismatch is the most common single cause of a failed setup, so install R first and read that page rather than reusing an Rtools already on the machine.

cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain() names the version it is looking for, and that is the version to install. It becomes available once the next section has installed cmdstanr. Under cmdstanr 0.9.0 and R 4.6.1 it reports

Rtools45 was not found but is required to run CmdStan with R version 4.6.1.
Please install Rtools45 and run cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain().

Which version cmdstanr looks for is fixed in the installed cmdstanr rather than read from CRAN, so the two can disagree; the Recurring problems on Windows section covers that case.

R packages

cmdstanr is not on CRAN, so it comes from the Stan project’s own repository:

install.packages("cmdstanr",
                 repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev",
                           getOption("repos")))

bayesnec and the rest come from CRAN, and installing bayesnec installs brms with it:

install.packages("bayesnec")

The CmdStan installation

Confirm the compiler is configured first. On a current Rtools this passes without doing anything; fix = TRUE repairs the problems it can rather than only reporting them.

cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain(fix = TRUE)

Then install CmdStan. Three things are set here, and each of them has been observed to stop a fresh installation on Windows.

dir.create("C:/cmdstan")           # install_cmdstan() does not create it
options(timeout = 1800)            # R's default of 60 seconds is too short
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(dir = "C:/cmdstan")

The directory has to exist first. install_cmdstan() does not create it and stops with Assertion on 'dir' failed: Directory 'C:/cmdstan' does not exist.

The download needs a longer timeout than R’s default. The CmdStan archive is about 49 MB, and the timeout argument of install_cmdstan() does not govern the download while options(timeout) does. Measured on a connection delivering about 500 KB/s, the download failed with Download of CmdStan failed with error at the default and completed in 4.9 minutes at timeout = 1800, with nothing else changed. Set it in any case: it has no effect where the download would have completed anyway.

The installation path has to be a plain one. The default location is inside the home directory, and on many Windows machines, particularly ones managed by an employer, that directory is synchronised by OneDrive, where the CmdStan build fails. The same failure occurs where the path contains a space or a character outside the standard English alphabet, which happens where a Windows user name does. C:/cmdstan avoids all three. Installing there rather than in the default location asks for two things in return: the CMDSTAN variable set out below, and dir = "C:/cmdstan" on any later install_cmdstan() call.

Because C:/cmdstan is not the default location, R has to be told where to find it in every later session, and the setting it reads is an environment variable rather than an option. Run usethis::edit_r_environ(), or open .Renviron in your home directory, add the line below, and restart R. Without it, every new session reports CmdStan as not installed and the path has to be set by hand in each one.

CMDSTAN=C:/cmdstan

R reads .Renviron only when it starts, which is why editing it takes effect on the next session rather than this one. The variable is the only thing cmdstanr reads for this: in cmdstanr 0.9.0 cmdstanr:::cmdstanr_initialize() takes the path from Sys.getenv("CMDSTAN") where that is set and from ~/.cmdstan otherwise, and no option sets it.

The version number is not needed in the variable. Where CMDSTAN names a directory that is not itself an installation, cmdstanr takes the newest cmdstan-* installation inside it, so the line above survives the next CmdStan upgrade unedited. The by-hand alternative does need it, and this asymmetry is easy to trip over: cmdstanr::set_cmdstan_path() takes the path as given, so it has to be called as set_cmdstan_path("C:/cmdstan/cmdstan-2.39.0"). Given the parent directory it sets the path to that directory, leaves cmdstan_version() at NULL, and warns

Can't find CmdStan makefile to detect version number. Path may not point to valid installation.

The back end is an option rather than a variable, so it belongs in .Rprofile, and putting it there means it does not have to be set again in each session. This line applies on every platform.

options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr")

Recurring problems on Windows

A partly built CmdStan directory

Where install_cmdstan() fails, run it again with these arguments.

cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(overwrite = TRUE, quiet = FALSE, dir = "C:/cmdstan")

overwrite = TRUE is the part that matters. An attempt that fails partway through the build leaves a partly built directory behind, and a second attempt without overwrite declines to replace it, which produces an error resembling the first one. quiet = FALSE only prints more of the build output, which is worth having because the default output is truncated and does not identify the stage that failed.

Chains that do not start after an Rtools upgrade

A model compiles and cmdstanr then reports No chains finished successfully, which names neither a cause nor a file. The usual reason is that Rtools changed after CmdStan was installed. CmdStan builds its own tbb.dll, linked against the toolchain that built it, so a CmdStan built under Rtools44 requires libraries that Rtools45 does not provide: the model still compiles, and every chain then exits immediately with STATUS_DLL_NOT_FOUND. Rebuilding CmdStan resolves it.

cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(overwrite = TRUE, dir = "C:/cmdstan")

Anyone who upgrades R and Rtools after installing CmdStan will meet this.

The cmdstanr version and the Rtools it expects

Rtools is installed and cmdstanr reports it as missing. cmdstanr chooses which Rtools to look for from the R version, and that choice is fixed in the installed cmdstanr. In 0.9.0, cmdstanr:::rtools4x_version() returns Rtools44 for R 4.4.x and Rtools45 for every R from 4.5 onward, which is why R 4.6.1 is sent to Rtools45. Version 0.8.0 sent every R from 4.4 onward to Rtools44, so an older cmdstanr beside the Rtools that CRAN pairs with R 4.5.x searches for a toolchain that was never installed.

Install cmdstanr 0.9.0 or later, which is what the r-universe repository above supplies, and install the Rtools that check_cmdstan_toolchain() names rather than the one inferred from the R version.

Slow compilation

Windows Defender inspects each newly compiled program, and a compile that should take under a minute can take several. Excluding the CmdStan directory from real-time scanning resolves it, where the machine’s policy allows.

Compilation blocked by policy

Some managed machines prevent a newly compiled program from running at all. This is a policy decision rather than a configuration problem, and it cannot be worked around from within R. Resolving it needs whoever administers the machine.

macOS

These steps have not been verified on macOS. They point at the upstream instructions, which the projects themselves maintain, and the check in the Verification section is what settles whether the installation works.

  1. Install R from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/, choosing the build for your processor: the Apple Silicon and Intel builds differ.
  2. Install the Xcode Command Line Tools by running xcode-select --install in Terminal. Some packages also require gfortran, and CRAN’s macOS tools page states the current requirement.
  3. Install the R packages as in the Windows section above.
  4. Follow the CmdStanR getting-started vignette (https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html) for check_cmdstan_toolchain() and install_cmdstan(). The default installation path causes no difficulty on macOS, so dir need not be set, and no CMDSTAN variable is needed either.
  5. Put options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr") in .Rprofile, as in the Windows section.

Linux

Install R through the distribution’s package manager or from CRAN, together with the standard build tools: build-essential on Debian and Ubuntu, or the equivalent development group on other distributions. Install the R packages as in the Windows section, then run cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain() followed by cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(). The default path causes no difficulty here either, so no CMDSTAN variable is needed. options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr") belongs in .Rprofile as it does on Windows.

Verification

Two checks. The first inspects the toolchain and the second uses it, so run them in that order.

cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain()
cmdstanr::cmdstan_version()

A configured toolchain reports

The C++ toolchain required for CmdStan is setup properly!

and cmdstan_version() returns the version string of the installation R is using. An error from either is a toolchain or path problem, and nothing below will work until it is resolved.

The second check fits a model, and it is the one that matters, because it exercises the whole path: bnec() calls brms::brm(), brm() writes a Stan program, CmdStan compiles it, and the compiled program samples.

library(bayesnec)
data(nec_data)

options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr")
set.seed(333)
fit <- bnec(y ~ crf(x, model = "nec4param"), data = nec_data,
            family = Beta(link = "identity"), chains = 2, seed = 333)
summary(fit)

A successful run compiles one Stan program, prints the sampling progress of two chains, and returns an object of class bayesnecfit. Its summary() reports the four parameters of the nec4param equation — bot, top, beta and nec — each with an Rhat near 1.00, then a Further Distributional Parameters block holding phi, which is the precision of the Beta response, then the NEC estimate with its credible interval, and a Bayesian R-squared. Two chains are enough to show that the toolchain works. The other vignettes take the brms default of four, which is what an analysis should use.

With that fit returning, the modelling vignettes can be followed; Single model usage is the place to start.

Provenance

The Windows failures described above, and the measurements quoted with them — the 49 MB archive, the download that failed at R’s default timeout and completed in 4.9 minutes at timeout = 1800, the OneDrive build failure, and the tbb.dll linked against a superseded Rtools — are taken from the software setup module of the concentration-response modelling course at https://github.com/open-AIMS/cr_modelling_training, commit 9d05595, which records what was seen on fresh Windows machines during 2026. They are that course’s measurements and not this package’s.

Every statement about cmdstanr behaviour here was read from cmdstanr 0.9.0 under R 4.6.1, and none of it is a course measurement: the environment variable cmdstanr:::cmdstanr_initialize() reads and the ~/.cmdstan fallback; the resolution of a CMDSTAN directory that is not itself an installation to the newest cmdstan-* inside it, and the absence of that resolution from set_cmdstan_path(); the Rtools version cmdstanr:::rtools4x_version() returns; the text of the three messages quoted above — the toolchain success, the missing Rtools, and the directory assertion — together with the fact that install_cmdstan() asserts a supplied directory rather than creating it, and that check_cmdstan_toolchain() forwards fix = TRUE to the branch that repairs rather than only reports; and the timeout argument reaching build_cmdstan() and build_example() while the download runs through utils::download.file() and so honours options(timeout).

The Linux route was checked on 2026-09-11 by running the course’s verification script end to end, with R 4.6.1, brms 2.23.0, cmdstanr 0.9.0 and CmdStan 2.39.0. Two limits on that check: it ran under WSL2 Debian rather than a native installation, and the machine was already configured, so it establishes the end state and not the instructions that reach it.
